questions.question: What does linear independence say about the equation $\alpha_1v_1+\cdots+\alpha_kv_k=\boldsymbol0$?
options: The equation has no solution at all.
The vectors must all be zero.
There must be at least one nonzero solution.
questions.explanation: Linear independence means the only way to get $\alpha_1v_1+\cdots+\alpha_kv_k=\boldsymbol0$ is the trivial $\alpha_1=\cdots=\alpha_k=0$.

option_explanations: The trivial all-zero solution always exists, so 'no solution' is wrong.
Independence does not force the vectors to be zero.
A nonzero solution would mean DEPENDENCE, the opposite.

questions.question: A list of vectors is linearly dependent exactly when:
options: there exist coefficients, not all zero, giving $\boldsymbol0$
questions.explanation: A list is linearly DEPENDENT exactly when some non-trivial combination (coefficients not all zero) equals $\boldsymbol0$.
questions.source_support: A collection is dependent if some non-trivial combination equals the zero vector.

option_explanations: 'Only all-zero gives $\boldsymbol0$' is the definition of INDEPENDENCE.
Not every choice of coefficients gives $\boldsymbol0$.

questions.question: If $(v_1,\dots,v_k)$ is linearly independent, in how many ways can a vector $w\in\operatorname{span}(v_1,\dots,v_k)$ be written as $\sum_i a_i v_i$?
questions.explanation: Independence is equivalent to unique representation: each $w$ in the span is $\sum_i a_iv_i$ in exactly one way.
questions.rewrite_notes: Hand-authored explanation + per-option explanations (why each wrong option is wrong + the likely misread).
option_explanations: Independence rules out two different representations.
Uniqueness means not infinitely many representations.
Since $w$ is in the span, at least one representation exists.

Yes, if the list has at least two other vectors.

questions.question: The list $(v_1,v_2,v_3)$ is linearly independent. What about the sublist $(v_1,v_2)$?

questions.question: Which list is guaranteed to be linearly dependent?
options: A list where one vector is a scalar multiple of another
A list of two different unit vectors
Any list containing no zero vector
A list of two vectors with different lengths
questions.explanation: If one vector is a scalar multiple of another, they are parallel, giving a non-trivial relation — guaranteed dependence.
questions.source_support: Any collection containing a scalar multiple of another vector is linearly dependent.

option_explanations: Two different unit vectors can be independent.

Different lengths do not determine dependence.

questions.question: Why is any list containing $\boldsymbol0$ linearly dependent?
options: A nonzero coefficient on $\boldsymbol0$ gives a non-trivial relation
Because the list then spans nothing
Because $\boldsymbol0$ is longer than the other vectors, which is false
questions.explanation: Putting a nonzero coefficient on $\boldsymbol0$ (and zeros elsewhere) is a non-trivial relation equal to $\boldsymbol0$, so the list is dependent.
questions.skill_detail: why a zero vector forces dependence
questions.source_support: Any collection containing the zero vector is linearly dependent.
questions.rewrite_notes: b34: removed generator residue; leak-safe
option_explanations: 'No direction' is informal, not the formal reason.
The list can still span things; that is not the reason.

The zero vector has norm $\|\boldsymbol 0\|=0$, the smallest possible length, not the largest; dependence follows from the non-trivial relation $1\cdot\boldsymbol 0+0\cdot v_2+\cdots+0\cdot v_k=\boldsymbol 0$, with a nonzero coefficient on $\boldsymbol 0$.

questions.explanation: Extending $(v_1,v_2)$ by $v_3$ becomes dependent exactly when $v_3$ is already a combination of $v_1,v_2$, i.e. $v_3\in\operatorname{span}(v_1,v_2)$.

option_explanations: It is dependent only when $v_3$ lies in the span, not always.
It can certainly become dependent.
Any $v_3$ in the span causes dependence, not only $v_3=\boldsymbol0$.

questions.question: Can a linearly independent list contain the same nonzero vector twice?
options: No, because $v-v=\boldsymbol0$ gives a non-trivial relation.
Only if the vector space is finite-dimensional.
Only if the vector has length $1$.

Norm-length is a metric notion, separate from linear dependence: scaling $v$ to have $\|v\|=1$ does not remove the relation $v-v=\boldsymbol 0$, so the doubled list stays dependent at any length.
